specAnchors.text: explain the potential dangers of electrostatic charges, e.g. when fuelling aircraft and tankers (physics only)
explain some uses of electrostatic charges, e.g. in photocopiers and inkjet printers (physics only)

primer.text: Static electricity is a working tool in some machines and a hidden hazard in others. Photocopiers and inkjet printers steer charged toner and ink with charge forces; sprayers charge droplets so they spread evenly. The same build-up turns dangerous near flammable fuel, which is why aircraft get earthed with a bonding line during refuelling.

modules.title: Uses: photocopiers & insecticide sprayers
modules.opening: Photocopiers run a five-step charge choreography: project the page, let the lit areas lose their charge, dust the rest with negative toner, transfer it to paper, then heat it fixed. Inkjet printers charge their droplets for steering instead. Sprayers charge their output so droplets repel into a fine, wide-reaching mist.
keyPoints: Photocopiers project the page onto a positively charged plate.
Bright areas lose their charge; the dark text areas keep it.
Negatively charged toner powder sticks to the charged text and is heated onto blank paper.
Inkjet printers charge coloured ink droplets negatively so they land on the right spot.
Sprayed insecticide droplets are given like charges, so they repel into a fine mist.
Those repelled droplets also fall fast, attracted by Earth's opposite charge.

low.restatement: Charged ink and toner go where opposite charges wait; like-charged droplets push apart to spread a spray.
low.analogy: A magnet-controlled ping-pong ball: steer it by placing the attracting pole where you want it to land.
low.examPointer: Learn the photocopier steps in order — projection, discharge, toner, transfer, heat-fixing.

medium.restatement: Every use reduces to force control: attract where you want deposition, repel where you want dispersion.
medium.analogy: Traffic control with one rule: red signs attract cars to park, identical badge plates repel drivers into separate lanes.
medium.examPointer: Sprayer answers have two halves — repulsion spreads the mist, Earth's attraction speeds the fall.

modules.title: Dangers: sparking when fuelling vehicles
modules.opening: A big enough gathered charge jumps the gap: that jump is a spark, and near flammable vapour it is an explosion waiting for a match. Fuel rushing through a pipe charges itself by friction, so aircraft are wired to the Earth with a copper bonding line while they refuel — the charge drains away harmlessly.
keyPoints: A large gathered charge can spark across a gap once its voltage is big enough.
Sparks near flammable fuel vapour can start a fire or an explosion.
Fuel rushing through pipes gains charge by friction against them.
A bonding line — a copper wire to Earth — carries that charge away safely.
Charge prefers the bonding line's path, so sparking during refuelling becomes very unlikely.

low.restatement: Static builds up on fuel; a spark could ignite it; a wire to Earth lets the charge escape instead.
low.analogy: Letting a kettle boil slowly through a pipe rather than letting pressure build until it bursts.
low.examPointer: Danger answers name the spark, the ignition and the earthing fix — three sentences, three marks.

medium.restatement: The physics is a race: charge flows down the bonding line far more easily than it can force a spark through air, so the safe path wins every time.
medium.analogy: A fire exit next to a wall: everyone takes the open door, nobody dives through the brick.
medium.examPointer: State what the bonding line is made of — copper wire — as well as what it does.

glossary.definition: Current forced across an air gap by a large gathered charge.
The copper wire earthing an aircraft during refuelling, carrying charge away safely.
The negatively charged powder a photocopier deposits on the charged text areas.
Injury or death from electric current passing through a body.
